drills.q: A learning curve shows train and val error both plateau at 15% error from 10k to 200k examples with a small gap. What's the diagnosis and what should you NOT do?
drills.a: High-bias signature -- more data and more regularization will not help. Fix: more expressive features or model class. Do not add regularization (it would only make the underfitting worse) and do not spend a week collecting more of the same-distribution data.

drills.q: Derive why ridge's (X^T X + lambda*I) is always invertible even when X^T X is singular.
drills.a: Adding lambda*I shifts every eigenvalue of X^T X up by exactly lambda (shared eigenvectors). If X^T X has a zero eigenvalue (singular, e.g. perfect collinearity), the shifted matrix has all-positive eigenvalues for any lambda>0, hence is invertible.

drills.q: A teammate builds a hyperparameter grid for sklearn LogisticRegression assuming larger C means more regularization. What's wrong and how would you notice?
drills.a: C is the inverse of regularization strength (C=1/lambda) -- larger C means LESS regularization, so the grid's intended direction is inverted. Notice by sanity-checking that the smallest C in the grid visibly underfits; if the 'most regularized' end doesn't behave as expected, the direction is backwards.

drills.q: Why is lasso feature selection unstable when features are highly correlated, and what's the fix?
drills.a: Lasso's corner-touching mechanism arbitrarily selects one member of a correlated group and zeros the rest -- which one gets picked can flip across resamples/noise. Elastic net (combining L1 and L2) retains L2's grouping effect so correlated features get similar nonzero coefficients together, while still allowing some exact zeros.

drills.q: A teammate says 'L1 regularization in XGBoost gives feature selection just like lasso.' Correct this.
drills.a: XGBoost's reg_alpha penalizes leaf weights within trees whose splits were already chosen by a gain criterion -- it doesn't zero out feature coefficients the way lasso does, and a feature can still be used across many splits. True feature-level selection in tree ensembles needs a separate step like SHAP-based pruning, not just tuning reg_alpha.

drills.q: You're asked to add regularization to a production XGBoost model that's slightly overfitting on 500 tabular features. What do you check before reaching for reg_alpha/reg_lambda?
drills.a: max_depth, min_child_weight, and subsampling (subsample, colsample_bytree) usually have larger, more predictable effects on tree-ensemble overfitting than the L1/L2 leaf-weight penalties -- check and tune those first.

drills.q: How would you convince a skeptical teammate that more regularization won't fix a model's poor validation performance, without spending a week trying it first?
drills.a: Show a learning curve with training error itself already high and converged, with validation error at a similar level and a small gap. If the model isn't even fitting the training data well, regularization -- a tool for reducing overfitting (the gap) -- cannot address a problem that isn't a gap problem; it would only increase training error further.

drills.q: What does double descent complicate about the classical bias-variance picture, and how should you state it in an interview to avoid overclaiming?
drills.a: Past the interpolation threshold, test error can decrease again as capacity keeps growing (Belkin et al. 2019), which the classical U-shape doesn't predict. State it as a real, empirically documented phenomenon mainly in high-capacity models (deep nets, some kernel settings) -- not as a general rule that bigger models are always eventually better, since compute cost and inconsistent occurrence across settings argue against that generalization.
